A total of 209 individuals completed the survey, located in 37 U.S. states; Washington, D.C.; Guam; and the Marshall Islands. The results highlight several themes: • Contractors hire to maintain quality and keep up with workload. Top reasons to hire are maintaining quality (73% of survey respondents), replacing a worker (70%), and meeting new business demand (61%). If workforce programs support stable pipelines of workers qualified with the right skills and certifications, firms can maintain high-quality installations. • Skill gaps, and the need to keep up with new technologies, codes or certifications are key motivation for contractors to invest in upskilling their existing workers rather than hiring new staff. Workforce programs focused on these areas may be more effective if marketed to contractors as upskilling opportunities for existing workers versus investing in programs for new workers. • Hiring is difficult largely due to skill and experience shortages. Lack of technical skills and experience was the most commonly cited barrier to hiring. If training programs include hands-on experience, companies can fill roles faster and complete more energy upgrades that lower consumer bills. Contractors prefer training workers when skill gaps are small. Companies often train when workers show reliability, fit, or only need incremental upskilling (mentioned 24 times). If workforce programs offer modular, short- duration training aligned with real job tasks, then companies can retain workers, build internal expertise, and strengthen the resilience of the U.S. workforce. • Cost is the main barrier to training—even when companies see its value. Sixty percent of respondents cited the cost of training as the primary or secondary reason they do not regularly train workers. Programs that reduce direct expenses or lost productivity might encourage firms to invest more in skill development, supporting a larger, more capable workforce. v This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. • Contractors prefer hands-on, on-the-job training. If offered training subsidies, respondents most frequently said that they would prefer funding for on-the-job learning (37% of respondents). This was followed by in-person certification courses and testing, preferred by 35% of respondents. • Many companies report that large shares of their workforce are not well trained. Less than half of respondents said at least 70% of their workers are well trained; gaps still exist in hands-on proficiency, safety, and soft skills. • Workers often leave to start their own businesses. Fifty-nine percent cited employees leaving to start new companies as a top reason for turnover.Training that expands entrepreneurial capacity in a supportive ecosystem may benefit regions as a whole, as the contractor base is more distributed and resilient. This also underscores the importance of recruiting and adequately training new workers to ensure continued high-quality work as experienced workers venture out to start their own businesses.
